1.6: Pillar number one: TANSTAAFL—so grammatically bad—"there ain't no such thing as a free lunch." Pillar number two: Incentives matter; incentives affect behavior. Pillar number three: Economic thinking is thinking on the margin. That might sound a little funny, but it won't once we cover it. Pillar number four: The only way to create wealth is to move resources from a lower-valued to a higher-valued use. There's a corollary there, which is that both sides gain from exchange. Pillar number five: Information is valuable and costly, and most information that's valuable is inherently decentralized.
1.7: Pillar number six: Every action has unintended consequences. Another way of saying that is, you can never do only one thing. Pillar number seven: The value of a good or service is subjective. 1.8: Pillar number one: TANSTAAFL—"There ain't no such thing as a free lunch." There are two senses of that term. In one important sense, it's always true, and in another important sense, it's usually true. Let's look at the sense in which it's always true. There are trade-offs. If you want more of this, you have to give up some of that. There's no way around it. You can't have everything. That's the sense in which it's always true.
1.9: Now, there was a famous president who said this: "The cost of one modern heavy bomber is this: a modern brick school in more than 30 cities. It is two electric power plants, each serving a town of 60,000 population. It is some 50 miles of concrete highway. We pay for a single fighter plane with a half million bushels of wheat. We pay for a single destroyer with new homes that could have housed more than 8,000 people." Which president said this? Someone who's very well known for his role in the military. He helped win the war in Europe: President Eisenhower. So he understood TANSTAAFL. He understood that, when you want more of something, you have to give up some of something else.
1.10: Now, I said there's another sense in which it's usually true. Another way of saying it is, there's a catch. Someone comes up to you on the street and says, "I'm going to buy you a free lunch." None of you were born yesterday. What do you want to know? "What's the catch? What do you want in return?" Sometimes there's no catch. I'm in my 70s, and so far, no one has ever come up to me and offered me a free lunch without there being a catch.
1.11: My mother taught me a little saying. "Don't look a gift horse in the mouth." I don't know, you've probably heard that. And the idea is—I found out later what it meant; I just took it at face value—it turns out, a way to judge a horse quickly, his health, is to look at his teeth. I didn't know that until some years ago. And so the idea is, someone's giving you a horse, don't question it, don't check the health. That's what my mother taught me. Well, what would we say with our understanding of there being a catch? We would say, "Always look a gift horse in the mouth." You might decide you still want to take it, but you want to do your due diligence.
1.12: Pillar number two: incentives matter. This is one of my favorites. It just applies all over the place. These are all true stories that I'm going to tell you. The Soviet economy was a communist economy with completely centralized control. They didn't have a profit motive. They didn't have private property. All the factories were government-owned. So they needed a way to come up with artificial incentives.
1.13: This first story is about a Soviet glass factory producing glasses, the kind you drink from. And they, of course, want to have an incentive to produce output. The central planners in the Gosplan in Moscow said, "We will give you an incentive if, in a quarter, you produce more than X tons of drinking glasses." What do you think the glasses came out as? Very heavy, because that's a very quick way to produce those glasses. And then they said, "That didn't work. We will now give you an incentive. We will give you a reward if you overproduce your three-month quota by the number of glasses you produce." And what happened? The glasses came out very thin and very breakable.
1.14: There was another case—by the way, I'd remind you, these are all true stories from the Soviet economy. Nail, nail production. First of all, they say, "We're going to reward you for the number of nails you produce." So you get very thin nails. Then, "Oh, let's change it. Let's reward you for the weight, the tonnage of nails you produce." And so, you got very thick, heavy nails. There was a Soviet publication called Krokodil that made fun of this in a cartoon. It showed this big derrick holding up this huge two-ton nail. And someone says, "Comrades, we have produced our monthly quota." That was a way to— they didn't do that, but it is a true story that Krokodil had this cartoon because they understood it.
1.15: How people came from Britain to Australia, they were convicts. The people shipping them were paid by the number of convicts they took on board. That sounds reasonable, but this really bad thing happened. They got to Australia, and a lot of them had died en route. Between 1790 and 1792, 12% of them died. Why? Well, they got sick. "We're not paid to deliver live convicts," so they would just be left to die. Sometimes, if they were really sick, they'd be thrown overboard. Sometimes, they wouldn't be fed much.
1.16: And even though these were convicts, people cared, were somewhat humane about it. So the British government said, "Wait a minute. Let's change our way of compensating people who ship convicts. Let's have a bonus for each convict who arrives alive." And it dramatically changed it. The next year, 1793, 0.3%, three-tenths of a percent, of the people died. I mean, that's an order of magnitude drop because of that simple change in incentives.
1.17: This you see all over the place. I remember—I'll get to Admiral Rickover in a minute— but I remember, when I was reading economics, I was a math major. I discovered economics when I was in college. And I started reading it on my own, and no one ever said this in any of the readings, explicitly, but after about a year of reading economics on my own, I said, "You know what? Everyone's talking about incentives." That's what economists do. It was just maybe so obvious to them. Well, I'm a teacher. I want to make it obvious to you. Incentives matter.
1.18: There's a great example. I taught military officers at the Naval Postgraduate School from 1984 to 2017. So I liked to come up with examples that would apply to them. At the Naval Postgraduate School—as you can imagine, many of the officers were in the Navy, so some of them knew this; most of them didn't. They were pretty young. Admiral Rickover, who's known as the father of the nuclear navy, faced a real challenge back in the 1950s when he was getting submarines built. We have these submarines that we want to go very deep. Well, if you've watched Das Boot or any of those things, and you know that they go deep, what can happen? They can implode; the welds might not hold. So what he told the submarine welders is, "You're going to go on the maiden voyage, and we're going to go deep." That concentrated their minds.
1.19: A lot of you probably, maybe you've taken some economics, or you've never taken economics, but one of the big things in economics is a demand curve. Another is a supply curve. That's all about incentives. The demand curve is downward-sloping. Here's price on this axis, here's quantity on this axis; and so, at a lower price, people want to buy more. There's an incentive to buy more. The supply curve is upward- sloping. Here's quantity on this axis, here's price on this axis. At a higher price, people supplying it are willing to provide more.
1.20: By the way, that just simple, simple understanding leads—we'll talk about it in a later lecture—leads to understanding why price controls are so destructive, because they keep the price below what the market price would be, so people want more, demanders, and suppliers want to produce less.
1.21: Number three: Economic thinking is marginal thinking. It's not all or none, but more or less. So you hear people say, "Oh, when the price of gasoline goes up, people won't quit driving." And that's true. They won't quit driving, but they'll drive a little less. They might carpool, they might go to a store a little less often and do more shopping when they go—all those little marginal changes that matter.
1.22: I've got an example of this. Years ago, I was buying beer for my birthday party, and I was looking at the choices, and I like Heineken beer. And I saw that there were 24 for $22, which was what I was used to. But then they had a smaller size, 18 for $20. I'm standing there pondering, and just coincidentally, the Heineken guy who had just stocked it, looks at me, laughs because he thinks he knows what I'm thinking, and he came close. He says, "You're trying to figure out the average." And I go, "No, I'm trying to figure out the marginal." In other words, if I buy 18 Heinekens for $20, compared to 24 Heinekens for $22, if I go to 24, I'm buying six more Heinekens for only an additional $2. So of course, I bought the 24.
1.23: Thinking on the margin—it also matters when you think about things like marginal tax rates. We economists use the term "marginal tax rate." What you probably have seen is tax brackets. So, on your last few dollars of income, what are you paying on that? So a lot of Americans will look at their federal taxes and say, "Oh, well, I'm paying roughly 12% to 14% of my income in federal income taxes, not including Social Security." But if they look at the marginal dollars, the last dollars, they may be paying 22%, 22 cents on the dollar, or 24%, 24 cents on the dollar. That matters.
1.24: So let's say you're living in a nice area and you're doing all right, economically, and you get an offer to go to a less-nice area, but because of that, there's a bonus: there's higher pay. If you want to decide, figure out what you're getting to make that move, you don't look at your average tax rate; you look at your marginal tax rate. So if you're in a 22% bracket, and they're paying you an extra $5,000, well, you're going to pay 22% of $5,000, which is $1,100. And of course, I haven't even included Social Security, which takes another bite. It doesn't say you should move, doesn't say you shouldn't move. It does say that that's a good way to think about making those moves, if you're looking at the tax aspect.
1.25: One of the most powerful tools in economics—a senior colleague of mine once called this the tool—is to look at marginal benefit versus marginal cost. So you do some activity, and you're trying to figure out how much of it to do. Maybe it's exercise. Well, you've figured out a certain amount, and then you say, "OK, what's the marginal benefit?" What's the additional benefit from, say, another 10 minutes of exercise? And what's the marginal cost from, say, another 10 minutes of exercise? It's a very powerful tool for looking at that issue, and that issue is everywhere.
1.26: A student is trying to figure out, "What's my marginal benefit of studying more?" I get a higher grade. What's that worth? That's the marginal benefit. What's my marginal cost? Will I give up other things? I give up leisure, I give up whatever. When I taught this to my students, I explained to them, "You might decide, once you understand the power of this tool, that you're not going to go for an A. And so, in a way, you're showing a lot of economic understanding by not going for an A because it's too costly."
1.27: Thinking on the margin should lead us to reconsider a famous line that probably most of our mothers taught us: "Anything worth doing is worth doing well." Let's think about that. There was an economist named James Buchanan, and we're going to run into him with the school of thought he was in. And he said once, "A real test of whether you understand economics is, do you understand what's wrong with that statement?" There are some things that are worth doing, but they're not worth doing that well.
1.28: Now, if you're doing welds on submarines, that's not one of them. But how about, we have three cats, and we have these kitty litters. And some mornings I'm in a hurry. And after I've cleaned out the kitty litters, there's a little that they put over the edge, and I'm in a hurry, and I leave a little kitty litter on the ground, on the floor. That's probably a good decision if I'm in a hurry. It's back to marginal benefit, marginal cost. How bad is it to leave it on the ground and then get it the next time I change the litter or clean the litter?
1.29: The only way to create wealth is to move it from lower-valued to higher-valued uses. So think about physical production. One of the standard examples is agriculture. What do they do in agriculture? They take land, seeds, fertilizer, water, labor, machinery, do all those things, and everything turns out right, the output, the crop that comes out, is worth more than the inputs. They created value.
1.30: I live in Pacific Grove, California, and years ago, we had a Blockbuster. Remember those? And then a new way of getting videos came along, and Blockbuster changed into Trader Joe's. That resource, that outlet, that physical space, was moved from a lower- valued use—it had become lower value—to a higher-valued use.
1.31: Now, there's a corollary to that that really is as important as the pillar itself. And the corollary is that both sides gain from an exchange. Think about something you bought. You valued it at more than the money you gave up, or you wouldn't have bought it. The person who sold it to you valued your money as or more than what it cost him or her to make. So that person gained. Both sides gained. That is one of the most powerful principles in economics. Both sides gain from an exchange.
1.32: Now, one way to test a principle is to stretch it, to take an extreme example and see if the principle bends or breaks. I'm going to give you, to start with, a made-up example. You're out in the desert. You are dehydrating. If you don't get water, you die. You're crawling along on hands and knees, and in the distance, you see this sign: "Rita's Friendly Oasis." It's not a mirage. You get there. Rita's there. You say, "Rita, do you have water?" She goes, "Yes." "Oh, thank goodness. I need two quarts. And then I can rehydrate. I can make it to Addis Ababa and fly home."
1.33: She goes, "Fine. That'll be $50,000." I should add, you have an American Express card, no limit. What do you say? By the way, when I asked some of my military students, the Marines said, "I'd shoot her." And I said, "Well, you don't have a gun. You don't have a gun. And she does, so that's out." What you say is, "I'll take it." Why? Because you pay $50,000, your life is worth way more than $50,000. So Rita gains in the exchange, $50,000, probably minus a penny. You gain from exchange, the value of your life minus $50,000. That's a big gain.
1.34: In fact, there's nothing in the principle that both sides gain from exchange that says both sides gain equally. And in fact, it might be a little surprising, but let's think it through. Who gained more? You did. Because if you value your life at more than $100,000, you gained more than $50,000, and she gained a penny less than $50,000.
1.35: So why does this matter? It's a made-up point, but why does it matter? Because I've taken probably the most extreme example you can imagine of a monopoly. She's got a monopoly. Yet, even in that case, both sides gained. That's a pretty powerful principle. As I said, it's a made-up principle. I mean, it's a made-up example. Let's take one that isn't.
1.36: There are companies in the United States, Nike and others, that hire subcontractors in poor countries, that hire people there for as little as a dollar an hour, and sometimes they're 12-, 13-, 14-year-olds. Let's look at that case. Does the company that hires them gain? Yes. Here's the tougher one, but think about it: Do the people getting hired gain? Yes, they do. How do you know? Because they're there voluntarily; they took those jobs. So that's better than the job they would have had.
1.37: It was interesting because someone on NPR, National Public Radio, some years ago, went down to one of those countries. And you could tell from his report on the radio, he got a surprise. He was going to find all these horror stories. And what he found was people who were saying, "You know what I used to work in? Agriculture. And you know what that paid? Less." And this was in the hot sun. Talk about sweat. So they were better off. He talked to this one person who said, "When I go back to where I came from, where I worked in agriculture, people see that I've put on 30 pounds," and unlike with me, that's a good thing. And they say, "How do I get those jobs?"
1.38: One other thing about that, there was a bill some years ago pushed by a US senator to fine US companies that set up and paid these kinds of wages. And this producer, I think it was rugs in Bangladesh, decided to lay off 2,000 children, just because of his fear of this bill passing. And what did they do? Started hunting through garbage, started going into prostitution.
1.39: See, the problem we Americans often have is, we say to ourselves, "I wouldn't want those jobs. I wouldn't want my kids to have those jobs," and that's absolutely true. But those people are in very different circumstance. No one's offering them a green card. They're in those countries. I wrote a piece on this some years ago, back in the '90s, when this had become an issue. I looked at various groups in the United States that were pushing to limit what they called sweatshops. And I pointed out, "You're looking at people who have a bunch of bad options, and they've chosen the best one of a bunch of bad options. If you take away the one they chose, you're making them worse off." So the way I put it is, "Someone who tries to get you fired is not your friend."
1.40: And by the way, the whole idea of gains from exchange explains why it's so hard to fight the drug war. I mean, think about it. Drugs are illegal, fine. Someone wants to buy them, someone wants to sell them. That's a voluntary exchange. So if you are, let's say, the buyer, you aren't going to go to the government and say, "He cheated me on that transaction." And so, they're not going to find—and how's that different from other crimes? Well, let's say you get robbed, you are going to go to the cops and tell them. Let's say one of your family members gets murdered. You're going to go to the cops and try to get that person caught.
1.41: But this is a voluntary exchange. And that's why it's so hard to fight it. And that's why they get very intrusive in the drug war, checking people's bank accounts, having, when you bring more than $10,000 into a bank, having to fill out a special form, all that kind of stuff. So, as you can see, the whole idea of gains from exchange explains gains from exchange, why people gain, and it also explains a whole bunch of other things.
1.42: Pillar number five, which is one of the more subtle pillars: Information is valuable and costly, and most valuable information is inherently decentralized. Let's first of all look at the easy part of that: valuable and costly. If information weren't valuable, I wouldn't be paid to give these talks. People value it. If information weren't costly, I wouldn't have to be paid. So there's evidence right here in me, in this room, that information is valuable and costly.
1.43: The person who really drove this home, and we're going to get to see him when we talk about the second talk on the Austrian School, is an economist named Friedrich Hayek, who co-won the Nobel Prize in economics in 1974. This is in 1975. That's me getting his autograph. Now, he was involved in what was called the socialist calculation debate. He wrote a famous article in the 1945 American Economic Review, called "The Use of Knowledge in Society." We're going to talk about it in detail when I get to the Austrians, when I get to him.
1.44: His insight helps explain why the Soviet Union failed, why it was a colossal failure. Now, granted, he focused on information. Incentives mattered a lot, too, as we've already seen, but I'm going to focus on the information part. There was a book from a reporter named Scott Shane, who covered the Soviet Union. He was the bureau chief in Moscow for the Baltimore Sun. And from 1988 to 1991—so remember, in 1988, you got straight- out communism, '91, you're starting the transition. So he got to see it at a very interesting time.
1.45: Based on what he saw, he wrote a book called "Dismantling Utopia: How Information Ended the Soviet Union." I think it was one of the best books of the '90s. And I'm saying that, having even published my own encyclopedia. And here's what he said. He took the example of shoes. He said, "My informal survey suggested that some of the longest lines in Moscow were for shoes. At first, I assumed that the inefficient Soviet economy did not produce enough shoes. For that reason, even in the capital, Moscow, people were forced to line up for hours to buy them. Then I looked at the statistics. I was wrong. The Soviet Union was the largest producer of shoes in the world. It was turning out 800 million pairs of shoes a year, twice as many as Italy, three times as many as the United States, four times as many as China." Remember, China has a multiple of their population.
1.46: "Production amounted to more than three pairs of shoes per year for every Soviet man, woman, and child," so they got shoes. Here's the problem. "The problem with shoes, it turned out, was not an absolute shortage. It was a far more subtle malfunction. The comfort, the fit, the design, and the size mix of Soviet shoes were so out of sync with what people needed and wanted that they were willing to stand in line for hours to buy the occasional pair, usually imported, that they liked."
1.47: Here was his conclusion. "At the root of the dysfunction was the state's control of information. Prices are information." That is so key. "Prices are information—the information producers need in order to know what and how much to produce. In a market for a product as varied in material and design as footwear, shifting prices are like sensors taped to the skin of a patient in a medical experiment. They provide a constant flow of information about consumer needs and preferences. When the state controlled prices, it deprived producers of information about demand."
1.48: I mean, I had this little thing I'd do in my class, when one of my students nailed it, and I'd say, "I could hug you." Well, I could hug him. By the way, he moved from The Baltimore Sun to The New York Times, and he'd read about this tough question I'd asked one of George W. Bush's officials when he came out to give a talk. It got written up, and he wanted to know if it was recorded, and I said no. Anyway, I said, "Hey, I love your book. That was great, the way you laid out Hayek's insights so well." And he said, "Who's Hayek?" So this guy didn't come to it from reading academic literature; he came to it from seeing it in practice in the Soviet Union.
1.49: Another example of the power of decentralized information. September 11th, 2001, was a horrible, horrible day in this country. There were actually three bright spots on that horrible day. The first one: people evacuating the Twin Towers. The Port Authority, which owned those buildings, told people, "Don't get out of the building." And people kind of used their own information and their own gut feel, and a lot of them got out. I had a friend who had a friend, has a friend, I think he's still alive, who had his own little business, and he had 20 people. And when the first plane hit, he didn't say, "Oh, grab your computers, let's leave." He said, "Let's get out." They acted on their own decentralized information. They got out, and they all lived.
1.50: The second thing: grounding the planes. There were approximately 2,000 planes in the air over US airspace when that hit. And the plan, the idea that the—I can't remember his name, but the head of the FAA didn't wait on the White House. He just said, "Let's get those things down." And it meant you weren't going to be landing where you thought you're going to be landing. You're going to be landing somewhere else. And the air traffic controllers moved them from one space to another. They'd never dealt with it in their lives. All those planes got down safely.
1.51: Then, something interesting happened. A few weeks later, someone in the FAA said, "This could happen again. Let's have a task force to think about how we would deal with it in the future, because we did seat-of-the-pants this time." So they met for a couple of times, and then they said, "You know what? No. It'll probably be different next time if there is a next time. Look how we did, dealing in real time with decentralized information. You go to a manual, you're going to lose time, and it might be the wrong advice, anyway."
1.52: And finally, even though it was a tragedy, United Flight 93. That was the one that crashed in Pennsylvania. What was different? Well, first of all, the advice we were always given—I used to fly a lot in those days—the advice we were always given is, if you get hijacked, go along with the hijackers. You're going to get a free trip to Cuba. You're going to have this great story to tell your grandchildren.
1.53: But what was different on Flight 93 was that these people had cell phones, and they found out on their cell phones—which means, by the way, they broke a federal law by getting on their cell phones—and they found out what had happened with some of the other planes. So now, no, no, no, it's not a free trip to Cuba. If I were to use the language of game theory, I'd say "the payoff matrix has changed." You're going to die if you don't do anything. You might die if you do something. So do something, because it might work. Of course, it didn't work for them, which was tragic, but it did work for whoever would have been attacked. People think it would have been either the White House or the Capitol building.
1.54: So there you have five pillars of economic wisdom, and those pillars are behind a whole lot of economics. And often it's a few pillars together. So, for example, we were talking about communism and socialism and why they fail. Well, that's the information pillar number five. It's also the incentive pillar number two.
1.55: Also, why does price-setting in a communist society not work? Well, it's the incentive thing again. If you set the price too low, less is supplied and more is demanded. TANSTAAFL. You've got limited resources. Even in our wealthy country, we always want more, and therefore we have to make choices and we have to make trade-offs, and there's no way around that. Lecture 2: Pillars of Economic Wisdom: Part 2 At a glance — Pillars of economic wisdom, part 2.
2.1: In the first hour, we covered pillars one to five. This next hour, I want to cover pillars six to 10. Let's start with six: Every action has unintended consequences. Another way of saying that is, you can never do just one thing. You want to achieve goal X, so you take an action to do that, but typically, everything you do has other consequences. Sometimes they're good, sometimes they're bad, and they're often unintended.
2.2: There's this famous story, it might be apocryphal, about rats, a little town in England being overrun by rats. The town fathers or town mothers and fathers, the city council said, "We should have a way of getting people to get rid of rats." And they started thinking about what we call pillar number two: incentives matter. "Let's pay people to get rid of rats. Well, how do we pay them? They have to bring in a pair of rats' ears." So people did that. The number of rats started falling, and then the number of rats started rising. What was happening? People were breeding rats in order to get those payments.
2.3: That's kind of a funny story. This one is not— the Exxon Valdez, which spilled a lot of oil off the Alaska coast. When something like that happens, Congress will often say, "Let's change some law to give an incentive for that not to happen." So again, they're thinking pillar number two: incentives matter. So they said, "We're going to raise the fines for something like that, and we're going to increase the amount that the firms are liable for, civilly." It sounded like a good incentive to do.
2.4: Well, here's what happened. I'm going to jump ahead to this Wall Street Journal story. "Already, at least one international oil company has been parking the title to some of its oil in transit with a willing outside party, a company controlled by fugitive oil trader Marc Rich in Switzerland. Refiners are also shunning legal ownership until the oil they buy arrives at their plants, instead of accepting it in the seller's port as before."
2.5: Get it? In other words, if they don't own the oil in transit, they're not liable. And then at the same time, some shippers are getting ready to subdivide their fleets into single-ship companies, each with minimal assets, so there's less to take over in a lawsuit, to protect the rest of their operations from any one claim. 2.18: And by the way, just back to that, about gains from exchange. We often hear people say, "You should give equal value for equal value." No, you shouldn't. Because if you do, you wouldn't bother. So real income and real output are just opposite sides of a balance sheet. The way you make income is by producing output. There's no other way. Now, if two presidents in our history, Hoover and FDR, had understood this, we probably wouldn't call the Great Depression, the Great Depression. They're the ones who put "great" in "depression." 2.30: FDR comes in, in the midst of the worst part of the Great Depression, and he puts into law what Hoover had tried to do just with persuasion. 2.32: Pillar number 10: Competition is a hardy weed, not a delicate flower. When you read the literature on antitrust—antitrust laws are used to go after companies that are thought to be colluding or thought to be too big or whatever—you'll often read the people writing as if they think competition is like this orchid. It's really delicate, and we need the right amount of sunshine and the right amount of fertilizer and the right amount of everything, water and so on. Bad metaphor, bad analogy. Competition is a hardy weed. It just happens.
2.33: Why does it happen? Because let's say some firms are making huge profits. What happens next? Other people see this, and they want to enter the industry and make those profits, and that drives down the profits. So consumers gain, and we get more competition leading tolower profits, but still some profits, and consumers gaining. Profits attract competitors the way honey attracts ants.

2.36: I used to ask my students 30 years ago, "What monopoly upsets you the most?" And it was typically the cable company, because there was just one in any market area. Almost every question in economics you try to answer will draw on one or more of these pillars. 2.39: Let's talk about AI. AI will put a lot of people out of work, and then— here's what I think —they'll find other work. Can I say what it is? No, I can't. But what I can do is look at history. What percent of the labor force is employed in agriculture now, even though we export and sell to the world? 2%, because agriculture became so much more productive.

And they paid what for many of us would be two months' wages for that trip. And so, two companies came along that figured out a way around it. One was Southwest Airlines. 2.50: What happened was this: Senator Kennedy, Ted Kennedy, wanted an issue because he wanted to run in 1980 for the Democratic nomination for President. 2.51: Then we get the actual bill in 1978 that deregulates. We have much, much lower fares now. Are we scrunched in our seats? Yeah, we are. But when airlines try to increase that space a little and charge for it, most of us consumers say—by our behavior, not by our words—we'd rather be scrunched in those seats. 3.1: In this hour, I want to talk about the Austrian School of Economics. Now there were a lot of people in that school. For this hour, I'm going to talk about two of them, Carl Menger and—I think I'll say this correctly—Eugen von Böhm-Bawerk, both Austrians, very important in the development of economics. They were part of, especially Carl Menger, and we're going to see in a couple of minutes, was part of what's called the Marginal Revolution.
3.2: Prior to the Marginal Revolution, economists tended to buy into what's called the labor theory of value. Adam Smith, who wrote the famous "An Inquiry Into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations" in 1776, believed in the labor theory of value. David Ricardo, in the early 1800s, believed the labor theory of value. Karl Marx based his whole edifice, his whole system of thought, on the labor theory of value. So what is it?
3.3: The labor theory of value says the value of something derives from the amount of labor that goes into it. I want to let that sink in, to see if there's even an inkling of what might be wrong with that, but we'll see. So the labor theory of value says the value of something is based on the amount of labor that goes into it. Well, then what happened was the Marginal Revolution of 1871. Three people in three different countries came up with it, independent of each other, with basically the same idea.
3.4: I think Menger said it best. William Stanley Jevons in Britain, Léon Walras in France, Carl Menger in Austria. And here was the basic—there were two basic insights. Value is subjective. Does that sound familiar? That's pillar number seven. There's no such thing as intrinsic value. Value depends on the person. What you value will be different from what I value. Even if we value the same thing, the value we put on it will differ between us.
3.5: And there was another part—and here's where the marginal comes in—each unit is less valuable than the previous unit. You go to Taco Tuesday at a restaurant, and you're trying to decide how many to buy. You start with two. The third one, even though it's priced the same, you value a little less. The fourth one, you value less. So at some point, of course, the price exceeds the value, the marginal value, so you quit buying them. Hopefully soon, hopefully without way overeating.
3.6: Now, what was so interesting was that this insight, which, if you think about it, seems obvious, wasn't obvious even to the great Adam Smith. And here's why I say that. In "The Wealth of Nations," Adam Smith talked about what has become known as the diamond-water paradox. Here's what he said: "Water is so much more valuable than diamonds. We need it for our very survival. And yet, diamonds, per some weight, are priced at a huge multiple of water." He couldn't figure out why. What's wrong here?
3.7: Well, guess what? Menger and the other marginalists did figure it out. Water overall, the overall amount of water in the world, is way more valuable than the overall number of diamonds. But the marginal value, a little bit of water, is worth very little, because there's so much of it. The marginal diamond is worth a lot because there's so few of them. So actually, if you were to do a demand curve—I think I can draw a demand curve without freaking you out— here's the quantity of water and the quantity of diamonds. Here's the price. Here's the demand for diamonds. Here's the demand for water.
3.8: Why is the price you're willing to pay for that first unit of water so much higher than the first unit of diamonds? Because without that first unit, you die. But we got so much water, we're down here. So the value of a marginal unit of water is very low. Whereas diamonds are still expensive to produce, so we're probably here, with the supply curve there, and the price is high versus a very low price here. So overall, if you think of the overall value of water, it's very high. The overall value of diamonds is very low, but the marginal diamond is more valuable than the marginal unit of water.
3.9: So, they resolved that, and Menger was huge in that. So Menger is also thought of as the founder of the Austrian School of Economics. He refuted the labor theory of value because—well, I'll say more in a minute. And he used subjective value to show that both sides gain from exchange.
3.10: He also showed the value of middlemen. I live in Monterey. I live 20 minutes from Castroville, where they grow artichokes. When my daughter was about four, we were driving by and she asked my wife, "Is this where the artichokes live?" We buy artichokes. Do we drive even that 20 miles to buy artichokes? No, we don't. We go to Safeway. They are the middleman. And you use middlemen, middlewomen, whatever you want to call them, all the time. And he pointed out the value of that.
3.11: He also, as I said, refuted the labor theory of value. Capital and labor are used to produce goods. What, he said, if capital and labor are expensive but don't produce much value—right there, they're expensive, but they're not producing value, so there's something wrong with either a labor or a capital theory of value. One of his examples was using capital to store up drinking water in regions abounding in freshwater springs. You build up big reservoirs of drinking water where you've already got springs providing it essentially for free.
3.12: And I want to get slightly political here and give my modern example, which is the high- speed rail in California, which I think, by the way, if it ever gets built, will be called the medium-speed rail. It's used up lots of capital and lots of labor, like tens of billions. What's its value so far? Zero. There are no rides yet.
3.13: Even very smart people can get hung up on this, and that's why I've titled this next slide, "Are you smarter than a Harvard philosopher?" Because if you aren't, you soon will be, at least on this issue. This Harvard philosopher, I saw him speak up at Stanford a couple of years ago, a very smart guy, but here's what he said in one of his books. Well, let me give a background. He said this. In 1965—he grew up in Minnesota—he could go to a Minnesota Twins game and pay $3 for one of the best seats. The Twins' major star at the time was a guy named Harmon Killebrew, who earned $120,000 per year.
3.14: Here's what he wrote in a book in 2012: "The business of baseball has changed a lot since then. The current star player for the Minnesota Twins, Joe Mauer, recently [in 2010] signed an eight-year contract for $184 million. At $23 million a year, Mauer makes more per game than Killebrew made in an entire season. Not surprisingly, ticket prices have soared. A box seat at a Twins game is now $72."
3.15: So are you smarter—I'm not saying on philosophy, but on economics—than Michael Sandel? He doesn't quite come out and say it, but it seems, I read the page a few times, it seems that he's thinking that higher player salaries led to higher ticket prices. Is that what happened? A hint here: don't get sidetracked by inflation. Yes, there was a lot of inflation between the 1960s and 2015. But ticket prices and player salaries adjusted for inflation are much higher now. So that's not it. What is it?
3.16: Let's say those players were getting that huge money that Joe Mauer got, but people didn't value going to the games much. That wouldn't last long. What's driving the salaries of Joe Mauer and the other players is demand, demand to see them play. It's not that the labor cost is driving value; it's that value is driving players' salaries. So if you remember that, and you end up in a room with Michael Sandel, you've got something, you've got something on him.
3.17: Now, Böhm-Bawerk also was very big on refuting the labor theory of value. His example was wine. Wine grows more valuable with age, even with no added labor. It's valuable as it ages. Now, I think there are even easier examples, and when I went through their work, I couldn't find them using this, even though I had a vague recall they'd used this, but I couldn't find it.
3.18: But here's mine: two people are out trying to find gold. One pans for it all day in a river in California. We have a weekly called the Carmel Pine Cone, and every week there's a story about someone wanting this color roof or this type of roof or this garage. And there's this huge uproar. 4.37: I had one—well, I'll get to it when I talk about something else. But I'll just mention, I had one a few years ago, where I wanted to cut a branch off a tree that was threatening our house, and I had to figure out whether the branch was under 4 inches or over 4 inches. If it was over 4, I had to get a permit, and I might not get it. You know what I did? I went to a hardware store in a different town to buy one of those saws, so that the hardware store in our town wouldn't remember me. And on Labor Day morning at 6 AM, I went out and sawed the thing off, and this cop comes by, and he waves. And I measured, and it was three and three-quarters. But this is crazy. This is crazy, having to live this way.
4.38: So again, Hayek is talking about how the world works, how local knowledge works, but he's also saying, implicitly and sometimes explicitly, we should be allowed to act on our local knowledge. And then he says, "We need to remember only how much we have to learn in any occupation after we have completed our theoretical training, how big a part of our working life we spend learning particular jobs, and how valuable an asset in all walks of life is knowledge of people, of local conditions, and of special circumstances."
4.39: I've taught this article to all my students for my last roughly 20 years of teaching. And by the way, they had trouble with his Germanic writing style, these long sentences. So I wrote out notes on each paragraph to give them, to walk them through, and then it started working very well. And here's a question I asked my military officer students. You graduate from the naval academy or you graduate from officer candidate school or ROTC, and you get into your first job. On a scale of 1 to 10, where 10 is you are it, 1 is you know nothing, what did you know in your first job? The typical answer I'd get back is 2 or 3. You learn it on the job. Local knowledge.
4.40: He gives some great examples. "To know of and to put to use a machine not fully employed, or somebody's skill which could be better utilized, or to be aware of a surplus stock which can be drawn upon during an interruption of supplies, is socially quite as useful as the knowledge of better alternative techniques." We tend to hold scientists up there, but it's also the very practical people who really matter a lot.
4.41: "And the shipper who earns his living from using otherwise empty or half-filled journeys of tramp-steamers, or the estate agent," he's writing now in Britain, so he means real estate agent, "whose whole knowledge is almost exclusively one of temporary opportunities, or the arbitrageur," someone we're going to meet later in this hour, "who gains from local differences of commodity prices, all are performing eminently useful functions based on special knowledge of circumstances of the fleeting moment not known to others."
4.42: Now, he was criticizing economic planning in the sense of central planning, and he wanted to make sure people understood that he wasn't arguing against planning. So he said, "This is not a dispute about whether planning is to be done or not. It is a dispute as to whether planning is to be done centrally by one authority for the whole economic system, or is to be divided among many individuals." So, more on what he called circumstances of time and place, and what we economists in the Hayekian tradition call local knowledge.
4.43: "It follows from this that central planning, based on statistical information, cannot by its nature take direct account of these circumstances of time and place, and that the central planner will have to find some way or other in which the decisions depending on them can be left to the 'man on the spot.'" So now we have an apparent dilemma. "We need decentralization because only thus can we ensure that the knowledge of the particular circumstances of time and place will be promptly used." By the way, this isn't me talking, this is Hayek talking.
4.44: "But the 'man on the spot' cannot decide solely on the basis of his limited but intimate knowledge of the facts of his immediate surroundings. There still remains the problem of communicating to him such further information as he needs to fit his decisions into the whole pattern of changes of the larger economic system." So, there's a dilemma here. It looks like it might be chaos. Each of us gets to act on the basis of his or her own knowledge. But how does that mesh? Isn't there just chaos?
4.45: So, I call this the price system to the rescue. Free markets to the rescue. He gives this example of tin. The price of tin rises. Is it due to a decrease in supply or an increase in demand? Let me show you a demand and supply curve. Quantity of tin per year. Price of tin. Let's start out with the demand for tin and the supply of tin. This price, P₀, is the price at which the quantity of demand equals the quantity of supply. At that price, Q₀ will be the amount both sold and bought.
4.46: Now, the price of tin rises, so something must have changed. Either the demand went up because they found new uses, or the supply fell. Maybe there was a strike in Bolivia where they produced tin, and we don't know. So for example, if it's the demand rising, we get this price, P₁, and more tin produced. If there's a strike that's causing the supply of tin to fall, we get S₁, and with the original demand curve, this price. Both are above P₀. So, the price of tin rises.
4.47: If there were a central planner who wanted to do a good job, what would that central planner want users of tin to do? Use less. But how would the central planner know: should we use less tin in tin pots, or should we use less tin in tin cans? The central planner wouldn't know that. But each user has his local knowledge. Each user says, "I can tell, if the price of tin rises, how to cut back on my use of tin." It does not matter for our purpose, and it is very significant that it does not matter which of these two causes has made tin more scarce. Because either way, whatever it is, I, as the tin-user, don't need to know that. I can adjust optimally in a way that no central planner could do, because he uses the word marvel.
4.48: He says, "The marvel is that in a case like that, of a scarcity of one raw material, without an order being issued, without more than perhaps a handful of people knowing the cause, tens of thousands of people whose identity could not be ascertained by months of investigation are made to use the material or its products more sparingly; that is, they move in the right direction. This is enough of a marvel, even if in a constantly changing world, not all will hit it off so perfectly that their profit rates will always be maintained at the same constant or normal level."
4.49: And then he explains his use of the word marvel. "I have deliberately used the word 'marvel' to shock the reader out of the complacency with which we often take the working of this mechanism for granted. I am convinced that if it were the result," the price system that does this, "if it were the result of deliberate human design, and if the people guided by the price changes understood that their decisions have significance far beyond their immediate aim, this net mechanism would have been acclaimed as one of the greatest triumphs of the human mind." Or as I once put it when I was teaching this article, maybe the free market should have won the Nobel Prize in economics every year it was offered. So, that's Hayek's "Use of Knowledge in Society." I think of it as one of the 10 most important articles in the 20th century in economics.
4.50: Now, as I said, there's this Germanic kind of writing style. Hayek had a buddy named Leonard Read, who was the head of something called the Foundation for Economic Education. He always liked to boil things down in a way that made it more understandable. So he wrote a famous article in 1958 called "I, Pencil." And it's a little hokey, but I taught this to 30-year-old military officers who didn't think it was hokey. They loved it.
4.51: The idea is that the pencil is talking, and the pencil says, "No one knows how to make me." And that's a literally true statement. No one knows how to make me. It's the result of a complicated division of labor where the inputs into this little simple No. 2 Ticonderoga pencil come from about five or six different countries, and he names the countries and lays it out. And this whole price system just meshes these people's decisions. So it doesn't have all of what Hayek has, in his "Use of Knowledge in Society," but it's quite understandable.
4.52: There was a famous economic analyst named Howard Stern who illustrated this. I call this "Howard Stern on local knowledge." This was way back. He hosted Julie Cialini, '95 Playmate of the Year, and Stacy Sanches, '96 Playmate of the Year. And he asked them 10 questions. The first six were about things in current events and politics and so on and science, stuff like that. First three questions. "Who is the President of Russia?" Julie: "Gorbachev." Stacy: "Gretzky." Correct answer: "Boris Yeltsin." I mean, everyone knows Wayne Gretzky is the Prime Minister of Canada. Who doesn't know that?
4.53: "Define the meaning of NAACP." "Something, something for certified pianists. It's some police organization." Correct answer: "National Association for the Advancement of Colored People." Question: "Who is the inventor of the light bulb?" Julie: "I know Edison invented the telephone, but I can't remember the light bulb guy." Stacy: "I don't know." Correct answer: "Thomas Edison." Alexander Graham Bell was the phone guy.
4.54: Next three: "Who's the Speaker of the House?" Julie: "Gore, something or other." Stacy: "Bill Clinton." Correct answer: "Newt Gingrich." Question: "Define the meaning of the letters CIA." Julie: "I don't know." Stacy: "Certified Investigation Association." Correct answer: "Central Intelligence Agency." Question: "What is the center of our solar system?" Maybe a little hint in there, in the word solar. Julie: "The equator." Stacy: "The moon." Correct answer: "The sun."
4.55: Then, Howard turns for his last four questions to questions that relate broadly to the industry they're in. "What did the initials D. K. stand for?" Both knew it was the fashion designer, Donna Karan. "What is Cristal?" Both knew it was an elite champagne. By the way, I didn't know that. I buy the cheap stuff. "What car company has a model known as a 911?" Both knew it was a Porsche. "Whose face is on the $100 bill?" Both knew it was Ben Franklin.
4.56: What is this telling you? Here's a perfect example of two people having their local knowledge, knowing the kind of knowledge that matters to them. I've got to say that I've often wondered, when I look at our school system, I think our government school system is a massive failure. And yet, it hasn't resulted in as bad a result as I would have expected. And I think it has to do with local knowledge.
4.57: I don't know if you ever watched Jay Leno. He called it Jay Walking, where he'd go out and ask people questions about the world, and they wouldn't know much. "When was the Civil War?" "1700," that kind of thing. Well, it doesn't matter much to them. What matters is the knowledge they get in their particular job. I mean, I think it's sad that they don't know these basic things. But what's really neat is that we still have a very productive economy without their knowing that.
4.58: One of Hayek's other books that's very important in his contribution—and it's not just totally about economics, it's also about political systems—is a 1944 book called "The Road to Serfdom." A friend, a mentor, gave me my copy for Christmas when I was 18 years old, and I started reading through it, and I couldn't stand it because, in my view, he was too good-willed toward socialists. He dedicated it to "socialists of all parties," and he didn't do it ironically. He was trying to persuade them. And I guess I matured a lot because I then picked it up again at age 19, and I loved it.
4.59: His big point was that the roots of fascism and Nazism were starting to take hold in Great Britain. Because fascism and Nazism were all about—I mean, put the Holocaust aside, which is a huge thing to put aside—but they were all about the government making itself the decider on everything and people having virtually no power in their own lives. And he was seeing that happen with Great Britain, and this was his warning.
4.60: It was written the way Hayek writes, which was sometimes hard for people to access because of that Germanic writing style. The Reader's Digest digested it down to a very short pamphlet with pictures to make the point. That sold hundreds of thousands of copies, and people got it. And there were some reversals in a good way in Great Britain after the war. There was this central planning of property usage, and they backed off a little. There was a proposal to have the federal government in Britain tell people what jobs they could have, literally say, "You can't do this, you've got to do that." They backed off that, big time, and so it had a big effect.
4.61: And here's what he said about government power. The government's power is "a power which is newly created and which, in a competitive society, nobody possesses." Hayek points out that the power a multimillionaire—there weren't billionaires at this time—"who may be my neighbor and perhaps my employer" has over him, "is very much less than that which the smallest functionnaire," smallest government bureaucrat, "possesses, who wields the coercive power of the state and whose discretion it depends whether and how I'm allowed to live or to work."
4.62: I gave my example of cutting tree branches. The city official in Pacific Grove had this power over me that this major company, Home Depot, didn't. That's where I went and bought that little saw. They have zero power over me. Amazon has zero power over me. Walmart has zero power over me. But a bureaucrat whose name I don't even know in a town of 15,000 people has more power than they have over me. And that's, fortunately, just about cutting tree branches.
4.63: But how about if they decide whether you can set up a company? As I mentioned in a previous lecture, governments often decide, "You can't be in this business. You can't have this job. You can't start this company." One example, in California, we have forest fires. You know who they often use to help with forest fires in an emergency? Prisoners. They let them out of prison for a while, and they fight fires. They seem to think they do it well. They go back into prison. They serve their term. They come out. Guess who's not allowed to be a firefighter? Someone with a prison record. That makes no sense.
4.64: So, more on government power over the economy. He says, "Whoever controls all economic activity controls the means for all our ends, and must therefore decide which are to be satisfied and which not." And I think this is so often forgotten about socialism. If the government has total power over the economy, it decides everything.
4.65: He also had a chapter, and it was titled, "Why the Worst Get on Top." Why do we have some of the worst people in our country be in top positions in politics? He lays out why. He says, basically, they're willing to do fairly extreme things to keep their power, and they're willing to be demagogues and so on to get people spun up in favor of their ideas.
4.66: And he quotes the late University of Chicago economist Frank Knight's memorable statement, and I'm going to talk about Knight soon—his memorable statement that "the probability of the people in power being individuals who would dislike the possession and exercise of power is on a level with the probability that an extremely tender-hearted person would get the job of whipping-master in a slave plantation." There's what's called self-selection. Who wants to be on top? Who gets to be on top? People who are pretty ruthless.
4.67: Now, there was, I should say an economic journalist named Henry Hazlitt, but he was almost an economist in his own right. By the way, if I had to recommend one book for people who don't know economics, it's a book written by Henry Hazlitt in 1946. It's still relevant. You read the chapters and you feel like he wrote about something I read last week, and it's called "Economics in One Lesson." So Hazlitt was friends with both Mises and Hayek. Hayek moved to the United States. Mises had moved to the United States.
4.68: And I remember hearing this story. I met Hazlitt once; I didn't hear it from him, but I heard it from someone who knew him, that he was asked the difference in temperament between Mises and Hayek. And here's how Hazlitt answered. "You ask both of them: 'What color is that cab?'" This is in New York. "'What color is that cab?' And Hayek would say, 'Well, it's yellow, of course.' And Mises would say, 'Any fool who cannot see that that cab is yellow!'" So it's just like a difference in temperament that the two had. And I think that's part of why Hayek got more recognition, even though Ludwig von Mises was fully as good.
4.69: And finally, I want to talk about a modern Austrian. He's probably 90 by now, but he's still alive, named Israel Kirzner. And he had a few—his major thing he brought to the table was on entrepreneurship. I remember going through, just randomly, seven textbooks, seven economics, the introductory to economics textbooks that various publishers had sent me because I, as someone asked to use a textbook, if I choose that for 40 people, they make a lot of money.
4.70: I went through, and I looked in the index for the term "entrepreneurship," and in many cases, I didn't even find it. So I paged through, and sometimes they'd talk about it, sometimes they wouldn't. But it just was, at best, shoehorned in there in a paragraph. Why? Well, because in the standard textbook, the ideal kind of competition is what economists call perfect competition. What is perfect competition? Everyone produces the same thing. Everyone sells it for the same price. There's no advertising, there's no innovation, and I'm sounding like Ben Stein. How's that great?
4.71: Well, Kirzner said, "They've left out the role of the entrepreneur." And the key in entrepreneurship is what he called alertness, alertness to opportunities. And one of the big ones he talks about is arbitrage. An entrepreneur sees that the good is selling for $10 in this market, and over in this market it's selling for $15, and he calculates the cost of shipping it, and it's $2. So he buys it for $10, adds $2 to ship, sells it for $15, and makes $3. It's that kind of thing that actually makes competition work, because other entrepreneurs see the same thing, and they go and buy it. And now maybe they bid up the price to $11 here, and they bid up the price to $14 here, and so on. So entrepreneurship, especially arbitrage, is a very big part of the competitive story.
4.72: He also emphasized the idea of competition as a process, not the kind of end state you get with this idea of perfect competition. And he talked about two main aspects of that —the role of advertising and the alleged waste from competition. The alert entrepreneur must also alert potential buyers to the presence and, ideally, the attractiveness of the items he's selling. In other words, it's not a given that people know what's out there. Advertising tells them what's out there.
4.73: Doing so uses resources, but those resources are not wasted. Kirzner writes that, "Selling effort, including advertising, that alters the opportunities perceived by consumers, constitutes an entirely normal avenue of competitive-entrepreneurial activity." There's also this claim out there that competition is wasteful because people make mistakes.
4.74: Here's what he says about that: "The truth is that until the newly competing entrepreneur has tested his hunch about the lowest cost at which he can produce, we simply do not know what organization of industry is best. To describe the competitive process as wasteful because it corrects mistakes only after they occur, seems similar to ascribing the ailment to the medicine which heals it, or even to blaming the diagnostic procedure for the disease it identifies."
4.75: In other words, mistakes are part of the deal. Mistakes are part of the process in finding out what works and what doesn't. So that, in a nutshell, is the modern Austrians, modern in the sense they did everything in the 20th century, starting with Mises, then Hayek, and Israel Kirzner into the 21st century.
4.76: Is there people that have more of a tacit knowledge versus a local knowledge, because that's the way their brains thinks? Like I said, in patterns or rhythmic understandings of things?
4.77: Here's how I'll reframe it and answer that, I think, this way. Are there degrees of tacit knowledge? I think there are. By the way, though, tacit knowledge is local knowledge. It's just part of—so I know that I want a ride back to my hotel at the end of today. That's not tacit knowledge, but it's local knowledge. I don't know what I'll have for lunch, but when I see the menu, I will know. There's kind of tacit knowledge. I might have been able to tell you, but I didn't and couldn't maybe, until I saw it. That's what I would do.
4.78: I don't have a question, but I want to make a comment about what you were speaking on, Howard Stern. It's like, people of today, everybody's a genius when it comes to politics. But then when you ask them, "Recite the preamble to the Constitution," and the majority of them would be looking at you like, "Huh? What is that?" Or the rest of them don't know what it is. Or you ask them, "Since you know so much, then what's the three branches of the government?" They don't have a clue. They might name one. "Oh, the legislature."
4.79: They're struggling, standing there, two, three minutes trying to think of the other two. And it just amazed me when you said that the people know, but they don't know. There's certain things they can pick up and say, "I know this," like the basic stuff that you were explaining the ladies got all right. But they speak on stuff that they really don't even study on, but they act like they're experts at it.
4.80: Yes. So I take it that your claim that everyone's an expert on politics was ironic. Yes, that's right. They think they are, but they're not. And by the way, when we get into the school of thought on what's called public choice, we'll talk more about why people are very ignorant of what's going on politically and how it's rational for them to be ignorant. Lecture 5: Chicago School At a glance — The Chicago School.
5.1: The next free market school of thought I want to talk about is the Chicago School, named after, you might expect, the University of Chicago. There were a lot of major players. I could have had double this list, but I want to focus on what I regard as the most important and interesting ones. The first one was an economist named Frank Knight, who had a long career from the early 1920s to the early 1970s.
5.2: By the way, I went down to the University of Chicago when I was 19 and knocked on Milton Friedman's door, and he talked to me for 10 minutes. And then I went to Frank Knight's door, and I heard him kind of yelling at someone on the phone through his door. I'm not the kind of person who backs down. And I didn't knock. And I still regret that because, a year later, he died. I shouldn't say, "He died, laugh, laugh," but anyway. So I never got to talk to him.
5.3: Milton Friedman—I'm going to talk a lot about him—George Stigler, Gary Becker, Ronald Coase, and Sam Peltzman. Let me start with Frank Knight. He wrote a major book in 1921 called "Risk, Uncertainty, and Profit." One of the big things he laid out is that, when you see high profits in a firm, sometimes it has nothing to do with a monopoly. It has to do with risk. It's a particularly risky enterprise. It could fail easily. There could be a decline in demand. There could be foreign competition, whatever. Meanwhile, the people in that business have to make high profits to compensate them for taking that risk.
5.4: He was very clear on what risk meant. He was very specific. Risk, in his view, meant that you could assign an actual probability to things. So it was a 0.5 probability this would happen, a 0.4 probability that would happen. As opposed to what? As opposed to uncertainty. Uncertainty means you know it's not a sure thing, but you don't really have a clue about the probabilities.
5.5: I remember this study came out in a British journal, whose name escapes me, claiming that various vaccines led to autism. The Lancet was the name of the journal. And apparently, some people refuted it, said, "This is bad data," this and that. And so there was this discussion on Facebook I got into, where people were saying that those data have been refuted, and I wasn't challenging that. But they were saying, "Therefore, vaccines don't cause autism." And I said, "Maybe they don't, but I don't know." And this philosopher said to me, "Well, you're an economist. You put probabilities on things. What's the probability it causes?" I said, "I don't have a clue." "Wait a minute, you're an economist." "I don't have a clue." I said, "It's uncertainty." He didn't get it.
5.6: Frank Knight educated a generation of economists. So his writing was important, but probably more important was who his students were. In his class, one particular year in the 1930s, his PhD class, were Milton Friedman—who I'm going to talk about—George Stigler, and another economist who was a friend of mine but didn't make as big a splash. But that was in one class. And by the way, Milton Friedman's wife, Rose Director, and that was her maiden name, was Director, and because Frank Knight organized them alphabetically, Milton sat beside Rose and ultimately married her.
5.7: Frank Knight had this kind of—he was very controversial in things he wrote, and he liked to make extreme statements. And so he wrote this article, which I had a copy of in my library—it was just a typed-out copy, it wasn't in a journal or anything like that— titled "The Case for Communism: From the Standpoint of an Ex-Liberal." Now, that title requires a lot of unpacking. Liberal to him meant classical liberal, which is what we today generally call libertarian. He wasn't making a case for communism at all. He was expressing his despair about the way the world would go.
5.8: Well, here's an interesting story. A student in my class—this was about 20 years ago— came to me at the end of the quarter and said, "Professor, my great-uncle was an economist at the University of Chicago." I said, "Really? What was his name?" He goes, "Frank Knight. But I didn't want to tell you because he's a bit of a black sheep in our family." I said, "Let me guess why." I rotated my chair, pulled his article out. "Was it this, 'The Case for Communism from the Standpoint of an Ex-Liberal'?" He goes, "Yeah, we thought he was a communist."
5.9: I go, "No, that was just his style. In fact, he educated Milton Friedman. He educated George Stigler. He educated a lot of people who had a substantial role in advising the Reagan administration. You might argue that, without Frank Knight, we don't get Reagan's 1981 tax cut." And this guy went away feeling so good about his great-uncle.
5.10: Frank Knight also was known—and I should have brought it as a prop—Frank Knight was known for, when he was working on an article, wearing this green poker hat, poker shade thing. He was very famous for it. In the mail one day, years later, shows up the green poker hat. He had retrieved it from his great-uncle's estate, so I still have it.
5.11: So, on to Milton Friedman. Here's a picture of me with Milton. Milton was shorter than me and bald. This was at a conference, actually, on Austrian economics in South Royalton, Vermont, in June 1975. I'm the one with the wonderful color combination of outfits, with my arms folded and my hair curly and long. That's Milton. I want to say a lot about Milton because, as far as the modern Austrian School, meaning the school of thought after, say, 1945, I regard him as the most important person for many reasons, both his contributions to economics and his contribution to public policy.
5.12: Milton Friedman revived what was called the quantity theory of money. I'll get into that in a minute. Let me tell you the background. John Maynard Keynes had revolutionized economics, the area of macroeconomics, the theory of the economy as a whole, things like inflation, unemployment, economic growth, from about the mid '30s to when his "General Theory" book was published, to the early 1970s. Milton Friedman harkened back to the monetarism that had dominated before Keynes and had lost some respect.
5.13: The quantity theory of money says, MV = PY, where M is the supply of money, V is the velocity of money, how quickly it turns over, P is the price level, usually measured by the consumer price index, and Y is real output. We call it real GDP, real gross domestic product. And that's not a controversial equation. It's actually definitional. This has to be true.
5.14: What do I mean then, when I say he revived the quantity theory of money? Well, in the Keynesian view, velocity moved passively, and you couldn't predict where it was going. In Friedman's view, velocity was more stable, and velocity is the inverse of the demand for money, basically. It's more stable. So if it's more stable, then you can say things about what happens when M goes up, when the money supply goes up, and if V is roughly constant, well, then this must go up. And then it's separated into price going up, price level going up, which is inflation, or real GDP going up, which is economic growth. That was what Milton spent a lot of his career on in the '50s and '60s.
5.15: So he wrote a book with a fellow economist named Anna J. Schwartz called "A Monetary History of the United States, 1867 to 1960." It's about a 600-page book, and they just track the money supply over that rough century and the various things that were happening, and correlating it with what was happening to inflation, what was happening to economic growth, and so on.
5.16: And the best chapter, the most interesting, exciting chapter, was the one that I reread a couple of times when I was studying for my area exam in monetary theory, was the chapter on the Great Depression. Because if you know some of the history of that, a lot of people attribute the Great Depression to the stock market crash in 1929. And they show that, no, that was not a major factor at all. The major factor was that the money supply fell by 30%. Well, if money supply falls by 30% and prices don't immediately fall by much, real output has to fall. So, they don't have the last word on the Great Depression. There's been more work done since then by an economist named George Selgin, whose book I reviewed that's really excellent. But nevertheless, they have a large part of the story of the Great Depression.
5.17: And then you have to bring in things they didn't talk about, but I talked about in one of my first two lectures, which is that both Hoover and Roosevelt, Hoover with persuasion, Roosevelt with legislation, tried to keep P high and wages high. Well, if you do that, you prevent them from falling, and you're going to get more of a reduction in real output. So that was a huge contribution.
5.18: The other thing Friedman is really well known for in this area is inflation. He made this famous statement, "Inflation is always and everywhere a monetary phenomenon." Why? Well, let's first of all explain, look at the way you can make that tautological. Because inflation necessarily means a drop in the value of money, by definition, that makes it a monetary phenomenon.
5.19: But he meant more than that. He meant, you will not see inflationanywhere that's sustained, that goes on for a few years, without going back and seeing that the money supply went up. So, you see that this goes up, say, 10%, so we have 10% inflation in a year. The odds are almost 100% that it's because M went up. Again, that's kind of common sense now, but he made it common sense. The Keynesians really hadn't talked much about inflation at all.
5.20: By the way, one of the things he did, and others in the Friedman tradition have done, is look across countries and look at what happens when you have very high inflation, and there it's really obvious. So there was the famous German hyperinflation of 1921 and '23, when prices were doubling every week, and sometimes over a few days. What was happening to the money supply? It was going up roughly comparably. So it wasn't a surprise.
5.21: There was a famous story—well, here's a true story, and then there's maybe the apocryphal story. 5.32: So what are economists getting at? They're getting at something called opportunity cost. The cost is not just the budget, not just the money spent to hire people. A standard example is pollution, where I'm producing a product, and pollution goes in the air and floats down and harms people, and I don't take account of that. And he went through a whole lot of legal cases in that article—that's why it was in the Journal of Law and Economics —to look at how things like that have been handled over the years.

5.84: Do I foresee another depression, anything close to the Great Depression? No, I don't. Here's why: the unemployment rate in the Great Depression hit its peak at 25%. The closest we came was in the '73, '75 recession, the '81, '82 recession, and the 2007, 2009 recession. I don't have the numbers exact, but they were all around 10%. That's a pretty big difference. So no, I think they understand enough about not letting the money supply fall.
5.85: Having said that, let me tell you a true story. At Milton Friedman's 70th or 80th—he lasted till he was 92, I'm going to say 80th birthday—Ben Bernanke, who was chairman of the Fed, made this little tribute to him. He said, "Milton, you're right. We caused the Great Depression. We're sorry. We won't do it again." But then he's chairman of the Fed, and what's he doing? He persuades Congress in October 2008 to let them start paying interest on reserves to banks holding reserves. What does that do? Well, now a bank says, "Gee, I could lend it out and take a risk, or I could get a sure thing by holding the reserves and having the government pay me." So what should have happened is that the money supply should have expanded a little to prevent that, and it didn't.
5.86: So there's a guy who said, "We understand," but he didn't totally understand. But again, do I think we'll get something like 25% unemployment? No, I don't. Could we get 12? I think so. One last thing to add, it goes back to incentives. One thing not to do is to increase the length of time in which you give people unemployment insurance, because it pays them to stay unemployed. They get pickier about the kind of job they'll take. Lecture 6: Mainstream Economics At a glance — Mainstream economics.
6.1: Where have we gone so far? Well, we've looked at the Austrian School and the Chicago School, but there are more free market economists out there, even in what's called the mainstream. There's a big world out there. So what I want to do in this lecture is do a sampling of the mainstream. I could spend 10 hours on this, but of course, that wouldn't make sense. I just want to hit some of the highlights of people who are not thought of as part of the Chicago School, the Austrian School, or what we're later going to see as the UCLA School, just doing good economics that ends up becoming very critical of various government regulations and various government programs, and also implicitly or explicitly, very positive about free markets.
6.2: So, I'm going to talk about the Brookings Institution. It's kind of thought of as a left-of- center organization in DC, where there are two economists, both friends of mine who do work in this area. Harvard, where you have Edward Glaeser and the late Martin Feldstein. Dartmouth, where you have Douglas Irwin. Columbia University, Jagdish Bhagwati. UC Irvine, David Neumark, and Michael Clemens. And he's moved around, so I don't have his latest affiliation.
6.3: So I want to start with Robert Crandall. I've already talked about him. He's the one who did a study in the Journal of Law and Economics in 1989 with John Graham of Harvard. What they looked at, I've talked about, was that CAFE, the Corporate Average Fuel Economy law, reduced the weight of cars in the late 1980s and would continue to do so in the '90s by about 500 pounds on average. To put that in perspective, that's about a 10% to 15% drop in weight. The lighter the car, all other things equal, the more in danger the inhabitants are in a crash. That, they estimated, made lifetime fatalities for each model year 2,200 to 3,900 higher than otherwise over the assumed 10-year life of the cars. That's a substantial number.
6.4: Now, Crandall also looked at—we talked earlier about monopoly in the economy and how government is one of the major, the major, creator of monopoly. I happened to mention monopoly in the legal profession, with governments keeping people out from being lawyers. Crandall, in an article he wrote, said, "We need more lawyers," not something you hear every day, but he pointed out the role of the American Bar Association in accreditation and how slowly they move in allowing and accrediting new law schools. And of course, if they move slowly on that, the law schools aren't turning out people who are accredited, and we don't get as many lawyers. So there's a huge premium to existing lawyers.
6.5: I talked earlier about externalities and how this British economist named Arthur Pigou, about a century ago, advocated taxes to use against externalities, negative externalities. But governments tend to use what's called command and control. They like to get in there and tell companies how to do things. So Crandall wrote a piece on pollution controls in "The Concise Encyclopedia of Economics," edited by that noted economist, David R. Henderson.
6.6: He gave this actual, real-world example. In St. Louis, there was a paper products firm and a brewery. They both put out pollutants that were somewhat comparable. The paper products firm, you could reduce a ton of pollutant for $4. The brewery, it would cost $600 to reduce a ton of pollutants. Under the regulation by the Environmental Protection Agency, the EPA required each of these to reduce pollution by some amount.
6.7: Here was the point that Crandall made: what if they'd been able to trade? What if you gave them some amount they have to reduce pollution, but if the pollutants are comparable in their harm, let them trade to either buy the right to pollute or sell the right to pollute. So let's take a simple example where each has to reduce pollution by a ton, and they can't trade. So, this one reduces pollution by a ton, and it costs $4. This one reduces pollution by a ton, and it costs $600. Total cost: $604.
6.8: But what if you allowed trade?
