So there was lots of pollinating of ideas, not just within Europe—within Britain, but also within Europe and across between the European continent and Britain. Very huge. It was very important that people be able to do these things across national boundaries.
8.21: At the same time, political fragmentation in Europe, that made it difficult for European governments to crack down. If you're in a city where the government is trying to crack down, that city government has a lot of power, but the next city over, they don't have as much power, or they're not cracking down, and you move over there.
8.22: Now, compare that to China, which cut itself off from the rest of the world. If you had been a Martian and you had come down to Earth in the 14th century and went around country to country and said, "Which country is going to make it big?", you probably would have said China. They were doing so many things right in terms of invention. And then their government or governments completely walled them off from the rest of the world, and they just lost out. So a huge part of what makes this work is cosmopolitanism, is sharing of ideas and goods and people across borders.
8.23: So there was an interview with Mokyr in 2009, and I want to quote some great quotes from that interview: "For the economy to function well, you don't just need good property rights; you also need what we would call, somewhat vaguely, economic freedoms. You need labor mobility; you need to get rid of guilds." Guilds were like occupational licensing. In order to practice a particular profession or a particular job, you needed the permission of people in that guild. "You need to get rid of monopolies." We talked about that, whether it be the Jones Act or other monopolies, both local and global. "You need to get rid of all kinds of regulations."
8.24: And here's what he says. "And above all, you need free trade." And then he said, "The more open the world is— the more free trade, the more ideas and people can move from one countryto another—the less likely it is that technological progress will come to an end." He is concerned about whether it will not necessarily come to an end, but slow down, and part of it has to do with things like restrictions on immigration. We might be losing out on a lot of good scientists coming from China, for example.
8.25: The guy who invented Zoom came over on an H-1B visa from China to Silicon Valley. He applied for a green cardnine times before he was accepted. I guess nine is the charm. And what would have happened if we hadn't had him? It doesn't take that many very productive immigrants to make a huge impact. So it is true that the immigrant who is running a restaurant or doing gardening or doing hairdressing or taking care of kids, those are all important, too. As far as technological change, these ones are really important.
8.26: So the moral of the story is that freedom mattered, and freedom matters. Now, we think of universities as being the place where ideas are generated. But I've got to ask this question: are universities—and the ones I know best are in America—are universities now places where people are free to pursue the truth without being censored or fired? And there's a lot of evidence that you can get in trouble for pursuing the truth.
8.27: I was at that Thomas Sowell event in October, where we were celebrating his work, and one of the speakers was a guy named Roland Fryer, an economist at Harvard University, a black economist at Harvard University. And he had won the John Bates Clark Medal. The John Bates Clark Medal is given once a year to the person who—I think it's in America, but half the economists are in America—the person who's the most promising economist under the age of 40. So it's on the level of the Nobel Prize. He's a curious person. That's the thing; if you're going to pursue research, you've got to be curious. You can't go in knowing what you want to find. You can go in thinking what you want to find. You can go in hoping what you want to find. But you've got to look at the data.
8.28: As I said, he's a black man. He did some research on whether police differentially killed, disproportionately killed, black people. I'm pretty sure he expected to find the answer was yes. He found the answer was no. He did find that police differentially treated black people badly, but not killing them. And there was a big uproar at Harvard, where he was, because of that. And then they discovered that he might have been involved in some kind of sexual harassment, which hadn't been talked about before he came up with that result. They really cut a lot of his funding at Harvard, and so this kind of stuff happens.
8.29: So again, the moral of the story is that freedom mattered and freedom matters. And that, in a real nutshell, is Joel Mokyr, the Industrial Revolution, and the hockey stick. Thank you.
8.30: In the 14th century, why did China cut itself off from the rest of the world?
8.31: In the 14th century, why did China cut itself off from the rest of the world? Real fear, real paranoia about foreign influences, and would they lose their culture? Would they lose various things? So it's not that uncommon for governments to want to do that. They were the extreme in doing that.
8.32: We need free trade. We keep hearing that over and over. What are the potential setbacks with free trade? And we were talking about this yesterday, but with free trade, how would you balance that out? For example, if we were wanting to get something from China, and it's more than what they want from us, would that be balanced? How would we make that work?
8.33: So, free trade, I'm going to answer about free trade in two parts. One is, are there downsides of free trade? Yes. But the downsides are no different from the downsides of things happening domestically. So, for example, China produces this very cheap electric vehicle. If the US government allows it in without tariffs, that will hurt a lot of domestic companies producing electric vehicles, and some of those companies will lose jobs. But if some producer domestically comes up with a way of producing electric vehicles more cheaply, other companies here lose market share, lose jobs. So there's no difference in principle or effect between the effects of free trade across borders and the effects of free trade within a country.
8.34: And now I've forgotten your second question. It was [inaudible], oh, yes. So one of the things people worry about, that economists typically don't worry about, is whether we buy more from a given country than they buy from us. I have this huge trade deficit with Safeway. I spend about $5,000 a year on Safeway. You know what those bums spend on my speeches and articles? They spend zero. I've got a $5,000 trade deficit. Why do I not worry? Well, everyone understands why I don't worry. They buy other stuff, and I sell my stuff to other people.
8.35: Well, similarly, it doesn't matter whether you have a trade deficit with a particular country. We have trade deficits with China and Canada and Mexico, but we have trade surpluses with a bunch of countries like the Netherlands, but it doesn't matter. Now, it is true that, if you add up our trade in goods and our trade in services, we have an overall trade deficit of about just under a trillion dollars a year. But where does that go? When they end up with that extra trillion, they invest it here, they buy US government bonds, they buy property, they buy companies, they make direct investments, setting up factories.
8.36: In 1988, Michael Dukakis was running for President. One of his big parts of his platform was to try to somehow crack down on foreign investment in the United States. He was really concerned about that. He went to a plant in a suburb of St. Louis, and he gave a talk about this. He said, "I know you don't want to be working for a foreign company, and we're going to try to make sure that doesn't happen very much." And some of the employees looked around quizzically. It turned out that what he didn't know was that they were working for a foreign company. Why is a foreign employer necessarily bad? I mean, they did all right with a foreign employer. And so, it's a lot of fear of the foreigner to some extent, which I think is unjustified.
8.37: Do you foresee technological progress coming to an end to some degree? And are you talking about more like AI and that kind of technological, or is it all of them, everything in general?
8.38: Do I see technological progress coming to an end? And what is the nature of modern technological progress? No, I don't see it coming to an end. I've always been kind of a glass-half-full person. I see ways that it will continue. Now, could the United States lose some of the edge if we regulate too much, if we don't allow more immigrants? Yes, but then it can happen elsewhere. But that's the great thing. A technological improvement, wherever it happens, we gain a little more if it happens here, but we gain almost as much if it happens somewhere else, because we get to still buy it or use it.
8.39: AI, of course, is the one people are talking about a lot now, and I do fear that it will be regulated in certain ways. There are these people who are thought of as being serious people—I just read one the other day, and I can't remember the name—who was saying that if we don't get our hands on AI and control it, it's going to take over within a decade or two and kill us all. Kill us. I don't mean metaphorically. I mean, it's going to be like Hal in 2001: A Space Odyssey, where it's going to just say, "OK, sucker, we don't like what you're doing. You're dead."
8.40: Now, do I know enough to say that can't be? No. But do I have enough native skepticism to say that's really, really unlikely? Yes. And by the way, if a government takes it over, what's to stop the government from using AI to kill us all? We do have a lot of experience with government killing people like the Holocaust, like Mao's China, and so on. And so, yeah, I don't fear AI the way a lot of people do.
8.41: I think that the median position of people who work with AI is more like mine. In other words, we can use it as a tool, and it's going to be very effective. So, yeah, I think technological progress will continue. I think Elon Musk isn't done yet, for example, and we'll get more from him. We'll get more from other people. So, yeah, I think it'll work out pretty well. Lecture 9: Public Choice School At a glance — The Public Choice School.
9.1: So far, we've seen a number of schools of thought, the Austrians, University of Chicago, the Chicago School, the UCLA School, and also the mainstream people who aren't really part of a school.
9.2: This is the final school I want to talk about: it's called the public choice school. Now, the public choice school is not free market per se. But if you look at their reasoning, their reasoning leads people to be more skeptical than otherwise about government intervention, and therefore, implicitly more favorable to economic freedom and free markets. The two most prominent members of the school of public choice were James Buchanan and Gordon Tullock, both of whom died.
9.3: Public choice is the application of the tools of economics to political behavior. James Buchanan, who won the Nobel Prize in economics in 1986 for his contributions to public choice, called public choice "politics without romance." In other words, I don't know if you've ever seen "The American President." I love that movie, but I love it as a romance. I don't love it in the sense that it's telling me much about the effectiveness of government policy in a good way. I even wrote a piece on that after the director was murdered very recently.
9.4: So let me say more about the public choice perspective versus the traditional perspective. Many economists, noting ways that free markets fail to deliver what they want, advocate giving more power to government. Most of them take what Harold Demsetz calls the nirvana approach, which we saw earlier. Public choice scholars say, "No, we assume that producers and consumers in the private sector are self-interested. Let's assume the same about politicians, bureaucrats, and voters."
9.5: Are we able, by assuming that and applying the standard tools of economic analysis to actors in the political sphere, to predict and understand behavior, and especially important, our pillar number two, incentives matter, and pillar number five, information is costly and valuable? These scholars who've looked at that, their basic answer is, "Yes, we can understand a lot of behavior that way." There are exceptions that I'll talk about, especially having to do with voters, but there's a lot of behavior that we can understand.
9.6: Here are two major insights from public choice. First, the individual becomes the fundamental unit of analysis. Public choice rejects the construction of organic decision- making units such as the people, community, or society. Bastiat, who I talked about, who is, in a way, an early public choice person without that term being used, once said, when someone told him society wanted something, he replied, "Bring society to lunch, and we'll talk about it."
9.7: Second, public and private choice processes differ not because the motivations of the actors are different, but because of stark differences in the incentives and constraints that channel the pursuit of self-interest in the two settings. For example, imagine a person buying a house. That person will look at the benefits of the house, what surrounds the house, what the neighbors are like, what the roads are like, what the schools are like, and takes all of that account in deciding whether to buy the house, versus that same person deciding whether to support a dam paid for by taxes, so they can get more water.
9.8: Well, now that person might come up with a decision. "Hey, I want the dam because my taxes for it will be less than the benefits." But other people might not want the dam because their taxes are greater than the benefits. So it's a very different choice. And that person will then probably look narrowly at whether, does the dam benefit me on net? Whereas with the house, it's, does the house benefit me on net? But the house is the whole decision. The dam is a bigger decision, and he just looks at how it affects him.
9.9: Now, one of the really interesting things that came out of public choice is what's called the median voter theorem. And the median voter theorem explains why the two main political parties are usually similar. It says this: if voters are fully informed, if their preferred outcomes can be arrayed along one dimension, for example, left to right, if each voter has a single most preferred outcome, and if decisions are made by simple majority rule, then the median voter will be decisive. The policy that wins is the one the median voter favors. This insight was from an early public choice person in 1958 named Duncan Black.
9.10: So, take a recent example. Kamala Harris and Donald Trump look pretty different on many issues. But look at two of the big issues: Social Security and Medicare, which together take a huge percent of the federal budget. Did they disagree on that? No. Neither of them wanted to do anything to trim Social Security and Medicare. As a test of the median voter theorem, let's see what happens when one of the major party candidates— the two-party system we have here—when one candidate positions himself far from the median voter. I'll take two examples.
9.11: One is Barry Goldwater versus Lyndon Johnson in the 1964 presidential election. Goldwater was more extreme on the right. LBJ was not more extreme on the left. So let's say we draw a bell curve of people's preferences, and it looks something like this. The median voter is here. And one of the big issues in the 1964 election, a huge issue, was Vietnam. It was early. Should we intervene in Vietnam? Goldwater was extreme on that. So Goldwater is, say, right here. In his view, I'll call it AuH₂O, Goldwater.
9.12: Now, if LBJ wants to do well, where should he position himself? A little this way, enough to look different enough, but then to capture a whole lot of the vote. So LBJ was somewhat hawkish. And the line at the time, the famous joke at the time, was this voter saying, "I was told if I voted for Goldwater, we'd bomb North Vietnam. So I voted for Goldwater, and sure enough, we bombed North Vietnam." Goldwater lost. That was a joke. So Goldwater got— sorry, LBJ got 61% of the vote, and Goldwater got 38.5%.
9.13: We saw something similar with Nixon versus George McGovern in 1972. There was a huge difference. Well, McGovern was very left on economic policy. He wanted something called "demogrants," where he gave everyone $1,000, which was a lot of money in those days. So again, the bell curve. Here's McGovern. Nixon's best strategy is to go different enough to look different and motivate people to vote, but not way different. And so he collects all those votes. So sure enough, Nixon got approximately 60% of the vote, 60.7%, and McGovern got 37.5%. So the median voter holds up. It's not a sure thing, but it holds up some of the time. It holds up when there's one main issue, let's put it that way, and two parties.
9.14: One of the other things that has come out of public choice is the issue of special interests, concentrated benefits and dispersed costs. We have sugar import quotas in this country that are very tight. In other words, our federal government limits the amount of sugar that can be imported from other countries. We have tighter import quotas than many other countries have. Of course, that makes the price of sugar domestically higher than otherwise. Our price of sugar is roughly two times the world price of sugar.
9.15: Now, 340 million consumers pay an average of $8 more each for sugar in a year. We lose, in other words. A handful of producers gain tens of millions of dollars each because the quotas drive the price higher, and those producers make out. Economists have shown that the loss to consumers is substantially higher than the gain to producers because we're getting very high-cost sugar, instead of cheaper sugar from other countries. So it doesn't pass a cost-benefit analysis test.
9.16: Why does it come about? Because the loss to each of us consumers is so low, we don't care much, and we probably don't even know about it. As a result, our voice in this controversy is a whisper, at best. When I've taught this, and I've asked my students, "Who knows what the quota in sugar is from some country?", they don't know the answer. Of course, they don't know the answer. It doesn't matter to them. But if you ask some of this handful of producers what the quota is, they'd be able to tell you.
9.17: By the way, one of the ways the inefficiency shows up: Coca-Cola. They don't use sucrose. They use— what do they use? Corn syrup. Coca-Cola, they use corn syrup, which is cheaper. By the way, I can go to Costco and buy Mexican Coca-Cola because they use sugar, because it's cheaper. Now, it's more expensive for me, but it's much better. And by the way, just one other interesting fact—and again, this gets to the issue of free trade—Life Savers, which used to be produced in Michigan, moved to Quebec, because they could get a major input, namely sugar, much cheaper.
9.18: So, special interests, concentrated benefits and dispersed costs: the producers gain a lot per person, so they have a very loud voice in the discussion. The consumers lose a lot per person, so they have a very quiet voice in the discussion, if at all. And this is just one example, but there's so many programs like this. This explains a lot of government.
9.19: I was talking earlier about occupational licensing and restricting who can do what and so on. If you look at the occupational licensing boards, state by state, they're made up primarily of people in that occupation who have a strong incentive to keep people out. If you look at subsidies to farmers, we have a couple of million farmers and 340 million food consumers and roughly 200 and some million taxpayers, paying for those subsidies. And so we, as taxpayers, as consumers, don't pay much attention. The farmers do, so they manage to dominate in the political sector. The participation is very lopsided.
9.20: So there's a book by a political scientist named James Payne called "The Culture of Spending." And what he did was, he looked at a whole lot of—he looked at 14 House and Senate committees in various years in the mid-1980s and looked at who testified in front of them, and what percent of them were testifying in favor of the government programs, and what percent were testifying against. 1,014 of them, or 95.7%, were in favor of the government programs. There were seven opponents, and they were 0.7% of the overall number of witnesses. So again, we see that lopsided thing in testimony.
9.21: Also, when public choice people started talking about these issues, they thought in terms of producer interests being the concentrated interest. But often, the concentrated interest is the government employees themselves. So here's the other thing he found: of the 1,060 Congressional witnesses mentioned, 673 were government officials, and 497 of those were federal administrators, and 65 were members of Congress. In other words, almost two-thirds of those testifying were government officials.
9.22: When I worked in the Labor Department, that was where I worked before I went to the Reagan Council of Economic Advisors, I would hear people who had been in that building a long time talk about the public. I came in with this idea of what the public were. And their idea of the public was whoever came and talked to them. So it typically was labor union officials and so on. It wasn't just what most of us would think of as the public. Again, that's the concentrated interest versus the dispersed interest.
9.23: Now, one way to see that this concentrated interest thing matters, I found two measures that I'd followed closely at the time, that I voted on in California. Here's the thing. Take any issue. If there's a vote, there's a chance that the median voter dominates. So if the issue is unpopular with the median voter, there are going to be more votes against it than for it.
9.24: There was a referendum in 1996 on Proposition 214 in California, the Health Care Patient Protection Act. This would have restricted health insurers' power to limit patient care. Now, why did health insurers want to do that? Well, think about the incentives within the health insurance system. The doctor doesn't bear the cost of ordering tests. The patient bears only a tiny fraction of the cost. So the insurance company bears most of the cost. And the insurance company wants to somehow be a gatekeeper and say, "Well, is this test really necessary?" So they wanted to limit things like that.
9.25: Who were the major supporters of this initiative? Nurses and other medical professionals. In other words, not sick people. We had a referendum, as I said. The vote was 61.2% against and 38.8% in favor. So it went down. Insurance companies were now free to impose the limits they'd had. And by the way, we as subscribers to insurance gain somewhat because, of course, insurance rates are lower than otherwise to reflect those limits. So, the people who wanted those restrictions went to the California legislature, and they got the Department of Managed Health Care set up in 1999. It established a special department to provide stricter oversight of patient rights.
9.26: Concentrated interest versus dispersed interest—the concentrated interest wanted this. It's not a referendum. It's a decision made within the government by legislators. And the ones they're hearing from, the ones making the noise, are the ones who want this restriction lifted. They want it to be harder for health insurance companies to restrict what's paid for. So, they lose because the median voter doesn't like it. So they go around it as a concentrated interest and get the legislature to pass it.
9.27: Now, one of the most interesting things that's come out of this public choice literature is the incentive to vote. One person's vote among millions or even tens of thousands hardly counts. The odds that your vote makes a difference in a Congressional election or a presidential election, those odds are extremely low, especially in the presidential election. And therefore, lots of people don't vote, and that's completely rational. So if you measure the payoff to voting solely by the outcome, that would say, don't vote. Well, there's a bit of a paradox here, because people do vote. So that must mean there are other motives for voting.
9.28: One way is to express your opinion. "I voted." You wear that little thing that says, "I voted." Some people see voting as a duty. I did my duty. Some people want to be seen as a good citizen, and that might explain why they say, "I voted." By the way, when I vote, and I think I'm in the minority, I never wear that thing because I don't want to encourage other people to vote.
9.29: But even then, people are rational. They'll vote less if the cost rises. Before poll taxes were made illegal in Southern states, a six-dollar poll tax in 1960—that was a lot of money; that would be like $50 today—reduced the probability of an individual voting by 42%. So they still do respond to incentives. That whole idea of the gains from voting being so small has led to two terms that public choice economists use— rational ignorance and rational irrationality. Let me look at rational ignorance.
9.30: Because your probability of affecting the outcome is so low, you have very little incentive to be informed. A member of Congress or a presidential candidate takes positions on hundreds of issues, and you might know none of them, or you might know a few of them. You don't have an incentive to be informed because you know, at a gut level, your vote won't affect the outcome. But it's also led to this later concept that came along. Rational ignorance came along in the 1960s and '70s.
9.31: This later thing came along in this century: rational irrationality. The idea is that not only is there little incentive to be informed, but there's little incentive to think rationally. For example, this candidate looks good, this candidate's handsome, or this candidate is beautiful, or this candidate is ugly, and it's irrational to vote on that basis, but there's little incentive to think rationally. Compared to what? You're buying a house, for example. You have a strong incentive to think rationally, but the outcome isn't really affected by you, so you have very little incentive to think rationally.
9.32: Now, one of the things that has come along as a result of the public choice insights is the whole idea of "taming Leviathan." So Leviathan is this idea of this overarching, big, powerful government that controls a lot of our lives. And of course, the Founding Fathers thought a lot about that. That's why they had the Constitution with its division of powers. And they drew in a Frenchman named Montesquieu, who'd written a lot about this. So the idea is that you tame Leviathan with a division of powers, with checks and balances, and explicitly in the United States with the Constitution, which has a division of powers and has checks and balances.
9.33: You don't need to know a lot of history to know that the Constitution is often ignored. For example, Article 1 of the Constitution gives Congress the power to declare war. The Constitution is a set of enumerated powers, which means, translation, if the Constitution doesn't give you that power, you don't have it. And yet, we've had President after President after President make war without Congress declaring war, and often without Congress having any input at all.
9.34: Public choice, though, buttresses the view that we should have some division of powers. And public choice people get creative with some of this. So I remember one of them at a conference saying, "You should have two votes on Congress. You should be able to vote for a candidate in your district, and you should be able to vote against a candidate in any other district." So you might single out these high-spenders in some county or some congressional district, probably in another state, who you don't like, you don't like what he's doing or she's doing, and you cast your negative vote on that person, that would be an interesting one.
9.35: So there are a lot of clever things people have come up with that, of course, no one has done yet. So that, in a nutshell, is the public choice school. Thank you. Lecture 10: The West German Economic Miracle At a glance — The West German economic miracle.
10.1: We're ending with one of my favorite topics: the West German economic miracle. It's a case where ideas really matter. We've talked about schools of thought, and I've talked about how, in various ways, they were important in effecting various policies. Here's the clearest-cut case where one particular school of free market economic thinking mattered a lot. It's called the West German economic miracle, but in fact, it's not a miracle if you understand economics, if you understand the bad effect of price controls, the bad effect of high marginal tax rates, and so on.
10.2: Let me give you the setting. The setting is postwar West Germany's economy. Food production per capita in 1947 is 51%—half, in other words, of its level in 1938 before World War II started. The official food ration, food was rationed, was 1,040 to 1,550 calories per day. Industrial output in 1947 was one-third its 1938 level. That's 1947. Twenty years later, Germany's economy was the world's envy. What happened?
10.3: Well, there were two main causes: currency reform and the end of price controls. Let me say more about the price controls. Hitler's price controls were stringent. There was a death penalty for extreme violations. Hermann Göring imposed rationing in 1938. Germany, of course, loses the war, and the parts of Germany get divided up. The Soviet Union has one piece; the US, Britain, and France have other pieces; and the Allied Control Authority is made up of all four of those.
10.4: There's a funny kind of thing that happens with humans. They have status quo bias. They keep what exists. So the Allied Control Authority kept price controls, kept rationing, and kept forced labor, so prices in May 1948 were only 31% of their level in 1938. Now, if you don't understand economics, you might think that's good. No, that just shows how out of line the prices were, because the money supply was five times as much. So with five times as much money, and say, the same amount of output, you should have five times the price level, rather than one-third the price level.
10.5: Prices that far out of kilter with what the free market prices would have been are going to cause extreme shortages, extreme. Let me tell you how extreme. People were growing their own food, and they were bartering. The money wasn't worth that much, because people selling the goods for that money weren't making much, because the prices were so low. So what people did was resort to barter.
10.6: There was this American economist who wrote a book about it. He was over there observing it, an American economist named Henry Wallich. And here's what he said: "Each day, and particularly on weekends, vast hordes of people trekked out to the country to barter food from the farmers. In dilapidated railway carriages, from which everything pilferable had long disappeared, on the roofs and on the running boards, hungry people traveled sometimes hundreds of miles at snail's pace to where they hoped to find something to eat. They took their wares—personal effects, old clothes, sticks of furniture, whatever bombed-out remnants they had—and came back with grain or potatoes for a week or two." Remember when we talked about Menger—why money exists? Because barter is so inefficient. But of course, if prices are kept way below free market prices, money isn't going to be that valuable.
10.7: A German economist named Walter Eucken said that "barter reduced the economy to a primitive condition." But now we have a school of thought that comes along that's very important. I'm not sure how good my German is going to be. I'll try. It's the "Soziale Marktwirtschaft," or social free market school, based at Germany's University of Freiburg. It's kind of like the Chicago School of the same era. The members included the aforementioned Walter Eucken, Wilhelm Röpke, and Ludwig Erhard.
10.8: Röpke said, "We need to end repressed inflation." In other words, we need to end these price controls that are keeping prices down, making it look as if inflation is low, but there's no connection between prices and market prices. We need a currency reform to end inflation and price decontrol to end repression.
10.9: Ludwig Erhard said the same thing as Wilhelm Röpke. He had written a memo during World War II, laying out his vision of a free market economy. He made clear that he wanted the Nazis defeated. That takes guts. You're at a German university, and you write something that's out there, saying implicitly or explicitly, "The Nazis need to be defeated." That took guts.
10.10: Now, there was another side on this, the Social Democratic Party, and their main economic ideologue was Dr. Lothar Kreyssig. He argued against decontrolling currency reform. He wanted more of a British Labour Party or Scandinavian policy. And by the way, to put it in perspective, if you've ever seen "All Creatures, Great and Small," or other things like that of the postwar era, you hear them talk about rationing. Britain kept rationing and price controls until 1954, nine years after the war. So he wanted something like that.
10.11: What was the resolution? Well, General Lucius D. Clay, a US general, was military governor of the US zone, and he wanted non-Nazis, and they weren't easy necessarily to find. But Erhard had refused to join the Nazi Association of University Teachers, so that gave him points with Clay.
10.12: Also, Erhard was recommended by Konrad Adenauer, who, of course, later became the German Chancellor. If you do crossword puzzles, as I do, you'll see sometimes, "Name given to Konrad Adenauer, der Alte, the old man." Konrad Adenauer has a very interesting story that gave him his anti-Nazi credentials, big-time. He had been mayor of Cologne in the early 1930s, when Hitler was starting to consolidate his power. And when Hitler came to visit Cologne, Adenauer refused to fly the swastika. He and his wife were put in prison. His wife died in prison. He got out, obviously. But that meant that Lucius Clay could pretty much trust him as a non-Nazi, and even an anti-Nazi.
10.13: So, Clay, with the recommendation of Adenauer, made Erhard the director of the bizonal Office of Economic Opportunity. And here's what he did in a very short time: he did a currency reform on Sunday, June 20th, 1948. He substituted Deutsche Marks for Reichsmarks, and the money supply fell by 93%. So now it's more in line with prices. Also that Sunday, the German bizonal economic council adopted a price decontrol ordinance that gave permission against opposition from its SDP members, the Social Democratic Party members, to end price controls.
10.14: Erhard had a fun summer. He got rid of, basically, all the price controls. And on his own initiative, he abolished food rationing and ended price controls. And there was a journalist at the time who reported the conversation between General Clay and Ludwig Erhard. Clay: "Herr Erhard, my advisors tell me what you have done is a terrible mistake. What do you say to that?" Erhard: "Herr General, pay no attention to them. My advisors tell me the same thing."
10.15: Also, on the issue of rationing, Erhard had a confrontation with a US Army colonel the same month. The colonel said, "How dare you relax our rationing system when there is a widespread food shortage?" Erhard says, "But Herr Oberst, I have not relaxed rationing. I have abolished it. Henceforth, the only rationing ticket the people will need will be the Deutsche Mark, and they will work hard to get these Deutsche Marks, just wait and see." As you'll see in a couple of minutes, we don't have to wait long.
10.16: Also, they cut marginal tax rates. The top individual income tax rate going in was 95%, and they kept it at 95%, which sounds bad. But here's the big difference. That rate applied only to income above 250,000 Deutsche Marks annually. Previously, the 95% rate had applied to all income above 6,000 Deutsche Marks, so almost no incentive to produce. In 1950, after these tax cuts, the median-income German was in an 18% tax bracket. At that same real income in 1948, he would have been in an 85% tax bracket.
10.17: All this, by the way, was reported by a US economist named Walter Heller. That in itself is an interesting story. Walter Heller later became the chairman of the Council of Economic Advisers under LBJ, first of all under JFK, and then LBJ. He was seen as one of the main opponents of Milton Friedman on the issue of monetary policy. He thought monetary policy didn't matter much. But here's this guy, Walter Heller, saying it's good to have these tax cuts. And by the way, Kennedy, before he was assassinated, proposed cutting the top marginal tax rate from 91%, which is what we had, to 70%, and Walter Heller supported that.
10.18: And here's what Heller says in an article in the National Tax Journal in 1948. He said, "The reforms quickly re-established money as the preferred medium of exchange and monetary incentives as the prime mover of economic activity." I want to point something out. I talked earlier about hyperinflation in Germany in 1921-23, when prices went up millions of percent; and yet, people still used money. They had to use it quickly, but they used it.
10.19: The money supply was five times what it was before the war, rather than millions times more as in the early '20s. So you might think, well, money would be more valuable after World War II than during the hyperinflation. But no, what that shows is the incredible damage done by price controls, because price controls were not imposed during the hyperinflation. So money could still be used, and you could get it. You could get what you paid for. Whereas with price controls after World War II and the money supply just being five times the pre-war level, money was way less useful.
10.20: What were some of the other effects? In May 1948, before these reforms, absenteeism averaged nine and a half hours per week. Workers were spending time going out in the countryside and bartering, so they were taking time away from work. As early as October 1948, absenteeism averaged 4.2 hours per week. From June to December 1948, industrial production rose by more than 50%. Longer term, between the first half of 1948 and 1958, industrial production per capita at an annual rate tripled.
10.21: By the way, a personal story about Walter Heller: I talked earlier about Milton Friedman's role in helping end the draft. Well, there was this push to bring the draft back in 1979-1980, and I wrote an economist's statement against the draft, just a punchy one paragraph, and sent it to economists around the country asking them to sign it. And Milton Friedman signed and Alan Greenspan, later chairman of the Fed, signed, all these people.
10.22: I sent it to Heller, and I didn't get it back. So I called him up about two weeks later, reached his office at the University of Minnesota. His secretary told me he's out on the island he lives on in Washington State. She gave me his number. Isn't that funny? In those days, you could do that. So she gave me his number. I called him. I said, "Professor Heller, are you willing to sign this statement?" He goes, "No." I go, "Oh, that's too bad."
10.23: I always believe you try to get something out of someone, even if you don't get what you wanted. So, I said, "Why?" And he gave, I thought, a so-so answer. And then I said, "How come you moved to Washington State?" And he said, "Well, my friends accused me of trying to move as far away as possible from Milton Friedman." Milton Friedman, meanwhile, had moved from Chicago to the Hoover Institution. So I said, "That didn't work well, did it?" Nice man, though. Nice man.
10.24: The German economy is humming, and Erhard gets a reward. He becomes Germany's first Minister of Economic Affairs until 1963. And then he becomes Chancellor of Germany until 1966.
10.25: And now I want to tell another personal story: I became friends in college with this man who was about four years older than me, named Clancy Smith. Clancy knew everything. He'd read everything. His name doesn't imply it, but he was Jewish. And he had made peace with Germany because the people in Germany in the '60s weren't the people who did what those people did earlier to his relatives. He knew the whole story about Erhard, and Erhard, meanwhile, had become Chancellor. And this is in the late, in about 1966 or '67, he came to give a talk at Winnipeg, and I went to the University of Winnipeg, where Clancy went.
10.26: So Clancy went to see him speak. And on Clancy's wall is a picture of Erhard that's autographed. Erhard liked cigars; Clancy liked cigars; and Erhard is reaching for a cigar. "I don't have one." And Clancy goes, "I've got one. Do you want one?" "Oh, sure." And I just get such a kick out of that because nowadays, "Does it have an explosive in it?" That kind of thing. But anyway, he gave Erhard a cigar.
10.27: Now, in telling the story of the German economic miracle, I haven't said a thing about the Marshall Plan. Remember the Marshall Plan? It was to give money to these countries to help their economies again. Why no mention of the Marshall Plan? Well, at its peak in 1948 and '49, Marshall Plan aid was less than 5% of German income, so it wasn't that big a deal. Moreover, other countries had higher Marshall Plan aid and lower growth. Britain was one of them, by the way. Belgium recovered fastest and relied on free markets, and its recovery predated the Marshall Plan.
10.28: So here was a case where ideas mattered. This school of thought in Germany that was ready for what happened once Germany lost the war had a huge effect, and it caused the German economy to recover, and not just recover, but flourish. Imagine what would have happened with the road not taken. Imagine what would have happened if they hadn't got rid of price controls and rationing and hadn't got rid of conscripted labor. That would have been a very bad story, and they avoided that. So ideas really mattered. Thank you.
10.29: How many people did we help with the Marshall Plan? How many countries?
10.30: How many people did we help with the Marshall Plan? I don't have it in my fingertips. The Marshall Plan aid went to Germany, Britain, France, I think Italy. So if you look at the population of those places, it would be 200 million, 150 million. But you can't say that everyone was helped. Remember, it's government aid. One of the requirements with Marshall Plan money was sometimes you had to buy things from the United States. It was partly implicit subject to exporters. So the Marshall Plan, we hear good things about it, but it wasn't that big a deal.
